Submission: October, 30, 2026 RadioLink Main Website

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: • This datasheet documents the design and development of my individual subsystem for the Team 105 embedded systems project. It provides an overview of the design process from initial block diagram and component selection through schematic design, power budgeting, PCB development, and subsystem testing. The purpose of this datasheet is to document the engineering decisions made throughout the project and provide the information necessary to understand, reproduce, and evaluate my portion of the system.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
• Team 105 is developing an off-grid communication device intended to provide communication when conventional cellular or internet infrastructure is unavailable. The complete system is divided into multiple interconnected subsystems that communicate through a central control board using UART. Power and communication connections between the boards are standardized to simplify integration and testing.
  • My subsystem is responsible for audio output. The speaker board receives digital information from the primary control board and uses a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano to control audio playback. Audio can be generated using an external MCP4911 DAC, with the PIC's internal DAC available as a hardware-selectable backup. The resulting analog signal is processed by a custom MCP6004-based amplifier and complementary BD139/BD140 transistor output stage before being sent to the speaker. The subsystem also includes its own 9 V to 5 V regulated power supply, debugging hardware, and connections required for integration with the remainder of the system.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
• My primary responsibility for Team 105 is the design and implementation of the speaker and audio-output subsystem. This includes selecting the speaker and audio-processing components, designing the DAC and custom amplifier circuitry, creating the subsystem schematic and PCB, developing the power system and power budget, and providing debugging and test features for subsystem verification.
  • The speaker board interfaces with the team's primary control board through UART while performing audio generation and amplification locally. The design includes an MCP4911 external DAC, a selectable connection to the PIC18F57Q43's internal DAC for backup and debugging, an MCP6004 operational amplifier, and a discrete BD139/BD140 Class-AB output stage for driving the speaker. The board also includes test points, debugging LEDs, a pushbutton, and spare GPIO connections to support testing and future modifications.
  • The following sections document the development of this subsystem, including the block diagram, component-selection process, bill of materials, schematic, power budget, PCB design, and verification results.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This is a block diagram of my planned circuit for group 105. The main component that I have chosen for the project is a speaker, with an amplifier to help drive the speaker. As a team we decided to have power all be supplied by the primary boards VBUS, and then transfer that power over through the 8-pin connector on the boards. Similarly we are using UART as our main method of communication between boards, hence the RX and TX connections. We also determined that we are doing a wheel and spoke setup, meaning we have a singular main board, with all of the communication going through that board before heading off to other sections.

docs.text:
Table 1: DAC component selection

Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC) — Individual Subsystem

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.PIC18F57Q43 Internal 8-bit DAC$0 additional costPIC18F57Q43 Datasheet * No additional IC required No additional PCB space required No additional cost No SPI communication required 8-bit output is sufficient for basic tones and speech * Limited to 256 output levels Lower audio resolution than external DAC options Uses an internal PIC peripheral Option 2.Microchip MCP4911-E/MS10-bit SPI DAC$1.83/eachDigiKey Product Page * 1024 output levels Four times as many output levels as an 8-bit DAC 2.7–5.5 V supply is compatible with the 5 V system Simple SPI interface Buffered voltage output* Good balance between resolution and cost * Requires an additional IC Requires additional PCB space Requires SPI connections to the PIC* Requires an external voltage reference Option 3.Microchip MCP4921-E/SN12-bit SPI DAC$2.62/eachDigiKey Product Page * 4096 output levels Highest resolution of the three options 2.7–5.5 V supply is compatible with the 5 V system Simple SPI interface SOIC package is relatively easy to solder * Highest cost of the three options Requires an additional IC and PCB space Requires SPI connections to the PIC 12-bit resolution may be unnecessary for speech, tones, and alerts Requires an external voltage reference

Choice: Option 2: Microchip MCP4911-E/MS 10-bit DAC

Rationale: The MCP4911 was selected because its 10-bit resolution provides 1024 discrete output levels, compared with only 256 levels from the PIC's internal 8-bit DAC. This provides improved resolution for recorded speech and audio while maintaining a simple SPI interface and compatibility with the board's 5 V power system. The MCP4921 provides greater 12-bit resolution, but this additional resolution is not necessary for the intended speech, tone, and alert playback application. The MCP4911 therefore provides a balance between audio resolution, cost, and PCB design complexity.

Both the MCP4911 and the PIC's onboard DAC are included in the final design to provide redundancy during testing. A solderable jumper allows either DAC to be connected to the amplifier input. The MCP4911 is intended to be the primary audio source, while the onboard DAC provides a fallback if problems occur with the external DAC or SPI communication.

package 1 MHz gain-bandwidth product Approximately 2 V/µs slew rate provides better large-signal performance than the MCP6004 Very low input bias current Low quiescent current* Good specifications for speaker Less familiar than the MCP6004, potentially increasing implementation/debugging time* Offers limited practical improvement for this particular circuit despite its better slew rate

Choice: Option 1: Microchip MCP6004

Rationale: The MCP6004 was selected because it provides the necessary performance for the custom speaker amplifier while remaining compatible with the board's 5 V supply. Its rail-to-rail input and output operation allows the audio circuit to operate around the 2.5 V reference used by the single-supply amplifier, while its 1 MHz gain-bandwidth product is sufficient for the intended speech, warning tones, and other audio signals. Although the LMV324A and TLV9004 provide improved slew-rate performance, this additional performance is not necessary for the intended audio bandwidth. The MCP6004 has also been used in previous lab assignments, meaning I am already familiar with how to setup and use the component. The MCP6004 does not directly power the 4 Ω speaker; instead, it controls the discrete BD139/BD140 complementary transistor output stage that supplies the required speaker current.

Speaker — Individual Subsystem

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Same Sky CMS-1852-24SP4 Ω, 2 W Speaker$3.52/eachDigiKey Product Page * Very compact 18 mm diameter 4 Ω impedance is compatible with the selected amplifier 2 W power rating closely matches amplifier output 300 Hz–20 kHz specified frequency range Lowest-cost speaker option * Small diaphragm limits acoustic output and low-frequency performance Lower specified sound pressure level than larger options May provide lower-volume speech than larger speakers Option 2.Same Sky CMS-40504N-L1524 Ω, 2 W Speaker$6.23/eachDigiKey Product Page * 4 Ω impedance closely matches the PAM8302A 2 W rated power closely matches amplifier output Larger 40 mm diaphragm than Option 1 Only 5 mm thick 400 Hz–7 kHz frequency range is appropriate for speech and alerts* Good balance between physical size and audio output * Larger diameter than Option 1 More expensive than the smaller speaker 7 kHz upper frequency limit reduces high-frequency reproduction compared with wider-band options Option 3.PUI Audio AS07104PO-R4 Ω, 3 W Speaker$7.42/eachDigiKey Product Page * 100 Hz–20 kHz specified frequency range Better potential low-frequency reproduction 3 W rated and 5 W maximum power handling 4 Ω impedance is compatible with the amplifier Largest speaker may provide stronger acoustic output * Significantly larger at approximately 71 x 41 x 25 mm Most expensive speaker option PAM8302A cannot utilize the speaker's full power capability* Large size makes enclosure integration more difficult

Choice: Option 2: Same Sky CMS-40504N-L152

Rationale: The CMS-40504N-L152 was selected because its 4 Ω impedance and 2 W continuous power rating closely match the output capabilities of the selected PAM8302A amplifier. Its 40 mm diameter provides a larger radiating surface than the 18 mm alternative while remaining only 5 mm thick. Its 400 Hz to 7 kHz frequency range should be adequate for intelligible speech, alerts, and generated tones. The larger PUI Audio speaker provides greater frequency range and power handling, but the additional size and power capability are unnecessary for the available amplifier output.

is primarily limited by the 5 V supply Lower current gain at high currents can require greater base drive More expensive than necessary for this application

Choice: Option 1: STMicroelectronics BD139 / BD140 Complementary Transistor Pair

Rationale: The BD139 and BD140 were selected because they are complementary NPN and PNP transistors specifically intended for audio amplifier and driver applications. Their 1.5 A continuous and 3 A peak collector-current ratings provide sufficient current capability for the custom 4 Ω speaker driver without the unnecessary size and current capability of larger power transistors. The BD135/BD136 pair provides similar performance but offers little advantage for this application, while the TIP41C/TIP42C pair has significantly greater current and power capability than the 5 V speaker circuit requires. The BD139/BD140 pair therefore provides the best balance of current capability, physical size, ease of assembly, and suitability for the custom Class-AB output stage.

Voltage Regulator — Individual Speaker Subsystem

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.STMicroelectronics L7805CV5 V Linear Voltage Regulator$1.08/eachDigiKey L7805CV Product Page * Provides a fixed 5 V output Rated for up to 1.5 A output current Compatible with the board's 9 V input Through-hole TO-220 package is easy to solder and prototype Includes over-temperature and short-circuit protection* Previously used during class labs, reducing design and troubleshooting complexity * Linear regulation causes power to be dissipated as heat Less efficient than a switching regulator May require additional thermal management at higher current loads* Requires external input and output bypass capacitors

Choice: Option 1: STMicroelectronics L7805CV 5 V Linear Voltage Regulator

Rationale: Ultimately the decision to use this component came down to us having used it quite a bit for labs in class. I already have experience using the component, I know how to build a circuit with it, and haven't had any issues the multiple times that I have used it.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The speaker subsystem is designed to provide audio output for the RadioLink communication device through recorded speech, tones, and alerts. The PIC18F57Q43 communicates with an MCP4911 10-bit DAC to generate the analog audio signal, while the PIC's internal DAC is available as a backup through a physical jumper. The signal is biased around a 2.5 V reference and processed by an MCP6004 op-amp before being sent to a BD139/BD140 Class-AB transistor stage, which provides the current needed to drive the 4 Ω speaker. The board also uses its own 9 V input and LM7805 regulator to provide the required 5 V supply.

This design satisfies the need for reliable and understandable audio output while also making the subsystem easier to test and troubleshoot. UART allows communication with the main RadioLink control board, while the backup DAC provides redundancy if the external DAC or SPI communication has issues. Debug LEDs, a pushbutton, test points, and spare GPIO connections provide additional ways to verify the circuit during development. Together, these features allow the speaker board to reliably convert digital information from the main system into audible speech and alerts while remaining easy to integrate and debug.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A power budget was created to determine the current requirements of the speaker subsystem and verify that the selected power supply and voltage regulator can safely support the complete circuit. The board uses a single regulated 5 V power rail generated by an LM7805 linear voltage regulator from a 9 V external power supply. Current requirements were estimated for the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, MCP4911 DAC, MCP6004 operational amplifier, BD139/BD140 Class-AB speaker output stage, and debugging and power LEDs.

The estimated maximum current consumption of these components is approximately 416 mA. A 25% safety margin was added to account for variations in component current consumption and operating conditions, resulting in a design requirement of approximately 520 mA on the 5 V rail. This value was then compared with the 1 A capability of the LM7805 and the selected 9 V external power supply to verify that sufficient current capacity is available for the subsystem.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The completed power budget indicates that the speaker subsystem can operate from a single regulated 5 V power rail. After applying the 25% safety margin, the calculated maximum current requirement is approximately 520 mA. The LM7805 is rated to supply up to 1 A, leaving approximately 480 mA of current capacity beyond the calculated design requirement.

A 9 V external power supply capable of supplying at least 1 A was therefore selected to provide sufficient power to the regulator and subsystem. The BD139/BD140 Class-AB speaker output stage represents the largest portion of the estimated current consumption and will be an important area to verify during physical testing. The power budget demonstrates that the selected supply and regulator provide adequate current capacity, although regulator temperature and actual current consumption should be measured during subsystem verification to confirm the design estimates.
